impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not govern prior art date determinations under AIA § 102(d)(2)—is correct, or whether a reference patent can only claim an earlier provisional filing date if at least one claim of the non-provisional is supported by the provisional's written description.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that claims of the '409 patent were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further consideration. The case turns on whether a prior art reference patent qualifies for an earlier provisional application filing date under AIA § 102(d)(2), challenging the Board's precedential Penumbra decision. This ruling has significant implications for how prior art dates are determined in inter partes review proceedings under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners may benefit from a narrower application of prior art effective dates, making it harder for petitioners to use provisional application dates to establish prior art status in IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR may face greater difficulty establishing prior art status for references that rely on provisional application filing dates, potentially weakening invalidity challenges.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds in district court litigation that were not raised in a prior IPR petition but allegedly could have been discovered through a reasonably diligent search.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one ground and inadequate accounting for hindsight bias on the other. The court clarified the evidentiary standard for determining whether prior art 'reasonably could have been' raised in an earlier IPR petition. This decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel and preserves defendants' ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a more rigorous standard for IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to assert invalidity defenses in district court even after an IPR proceeding.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty using IPR estoppel to foreclose invalidity arguments in district court, potentially prolonging and complicating patent enforcement litigation.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's trade secret misappropriation claim under the Defend Trade Secrets Act was time-barred where the alleged misappropriation began in 2018 and suit was filed in August 2023, and what constitutes the accrual date for the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and district court judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The court determined that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing. This decision provides important guidance on the DTSA statute of limitations and the duty to investigate potential misappropriation diligently.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a strong limitations defense when the plaintiff had knowledge or constructive knowledge of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing claims if they delay filing suit, even while investigating, and must act more quickly upon discovering potential misappropriation to preserve DTSA claims.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether Ford was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on trade secret misappropriation liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the reduction of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating the original jury verdict. However, the court affirmed the finding of trade secret misappropriation liability against Ford. This case provides important guidance on permissible damages methodologies in trade secret cases under the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from broader acceptance of damages models, and the reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award signals deference to jury findings on damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop proprietary software after licensing from third parties face sustained liability exposure for trade secret misappropriation where they create competing products.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional patent constituted correction of an obvious typographical error entitling the patent to the provisional's priority date, or whether the change introduced new matter that broke the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment that Enanta's '953 patent was invalid as anticipated, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl group definition was not an obvious typographical error and therefore the patent could not claim priority from its provisional application. Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid) thus constituted anticipating prior art. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent priority claims and the strictness with which priority chain requirements are enforced.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical companies benefit from strict enforcement of priority date requirements, as even small discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications can break the priority chain and open patents to invalidity challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders face heightened risk that minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications will be treated as new matter rather than typographical errors, potentially invalidating valuable drug patents.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in using a single verdict form question covering infringement for all asserted patents, and whether asserted patent claims directed to wireless building automation systems were invalid under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents was reversible error. The court also vacated and remanded for further Alice step two analysis on the '495 patent but affirmed that the '887 and '371 patent claims were not directed to abstract ideas. This ruling reinforces the requirement for patent-specific verdict forms in multi-patent cases and provides guidance on § 101 eligibility for IoT/building automation technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement of patent-specific verdict questions, which prevents bundled verdicts that obscure the basis for liability across multiple patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face increased procedural complexity and the risk that flawed verdict forms will result in vacated judgments, even after successful jury trials.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of Federal Claims correctly assessed copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation methodology rather than deferring to an existing license agreement, and whether the court properly applied the 'book of wisdom' doctrine.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the use of a hypothetical negotiation to assess damages for the government's infringement of copyrighted software (TETRA) but vacated the damages award in part, finding that the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages. The case establishes that courts are not compelled to defer to existing license terms when calculating copyright damages against the government and clarifies limitations on the book of wisdom doctrine in copyright cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's endorsement of hypothetical negotiation as a valid damages methodology, potentially yielding higher awards than existing license rates.
impacts.negativeImplications: The government and licensees face uncertainty in copyright damages calculations, as courts may depart from actual license terms, but the ruling also limits speculative or non-compensatory damages.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patent claims were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, finding they claimed abstract data collection and processing concepts. The court also vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional, suggesting attorney fees may be warranted. This decision continues to narrow the scope of patentable subject matter for agricultural technology and data processing patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies facing patent assertions benefit from the confirmation that abstract data collection claims applied to farming contexts remain patent-ineligible, and may recover fees in exceptional cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on agricultural data systems face heightened § 101 invalidity risk, and the remand on exceptionality signals potential fee-shifting exposure for asserting such patents.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling based on a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of claims by a bank holding company and its subsidiaries that lost significant assets during the 2008 financial crisis. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in CalPERS v. ANZ Securities. This ruling has significant implications for financial institutions and investors seeking to bring claims against the government based on the 2008 financial crisis and GSE conservatorship.
impacts.negativeImplications: Financial institutions and investors who relied on class action tolling to preserve individual claims against the government face statute of limitations bars, particularly for claims arising from the 2008 financial crisis and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac conservatorship.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of claims directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber compositions used in coronary stents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's infringement verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL on both anticipation and non-infringement grounds for the '296 patent covering drug-eluting stent technology. The court found that the prior art fully anticipated the claimed composition and that UT failed to prove infringement as a matter of law. This decision significantly impacts the medical device industry, particularly the multi-billion-dollar drug-eluting stent market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies like Boston Scientific benefit from the reversal of a potentially large damages judgment and the clarification that broad composition claims in the stent field may be vulnerable to anticipation challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and research institutions holding composition patents in the medical device space face heightened risk that their broad claims will be invalidated by prior art, undermining licensing revenue.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's en banc decision in Egyptian Goddess improperly shifted the design patent infringement inquiry to focus on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality questions in design patent claim construction should be decided by the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied rehearing en banc in a design patent case, but the split decision—with a vigorous dissent from Chief Judge Moore joined by Judge Reyna, plus silent dissents from Judges Stoll and Stark—signals deep division on the proper framework for design patent infringement. The dissent argued that Egyptian Goddess has been misapplied to improperly resolve infringement at summary judgment and to remove functionality questions from jury consideration. This denial preserves the current framework but highlights ongoing controversy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the preserved ability to defeat design patent claims at summary judgment based on visual differences between designs without a full trial.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that courts will resolve infringement at summary judgment by focusing on design differences, and the four-judge dissent signals potential future instability in design patent law.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation to refer to the free base forms rather than salt forms, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic competitor to Nuedexta (treating pseudobulbar affect) but vacated the district court's waiver of the bond requirement pending appeal. The court upheld the claim construction interpreting drug terms in the weight-to-weight ratio as referring to free base forms. This decision has significant implications for Hatch-Waxman litigation and the enforceability of pharmaceutical method-of-treatment patents near expiration.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmation of preliminary injunctions blocking generic entry and claim constructions covering salt forms of drugs, protecting revenue during the final months of patent life.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face injunctions delaying market entry even near patent expiration, and the bond requirement on appeal adds financial exposure for brand companies seeking preliminary relief.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish Article III constitutional standing to sue for patent infringement when it retains the right to sue third parties.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner retains constitutional standing to sue for infringement when it reserves the right to bring infringement actions against third parties, even after granting an exclusive license to another entity. The court found that the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the licensee's rights. This decision clarifies standing requirements for patent owners who have entered complex licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license their patents exclusively but retain litigation rights can continue to enforce their patents, providing flexibility in structuring licensing agreements while preserving enforcement ability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potentially dispositive standing defense when patent owners retain the contractual right to sue, even where the patent owner has granted broad exclusive licenses.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds where all but four claims had been invalidated in IPR, and whether attorney fees under § 285 and sanctions under § 1927 were warranted.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of the patent infringement complaint but reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and the § 1927 attorney sanction, finding insufficient grounds to support either. The court held that the surviving claims were invalid on the same obviousness grounds as the cancelled claims but that bringing suit on surviving claims was not objectively baseless. This decision clarifies the boundaries of exceptional case findings and attorney sanctions in patent cases following partial IPR invalidation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders and their counsel benefit from the reversal of fee-shifting and sanctions, establishing that asserting claims that survived IPR is not per se exceptional or sanctionable even when those claims are ultimately invalidated.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers who successfully defend against weakened patents post-IPR may find it harder to recover fees and costs, even in cases where the remaining claims are ultimately found invalid.
